drills.q: Why does a metadata filter break both pre-filtering and post-filtering when applied to an ANN index?
drills.a: Every ANN index is built assuming any indexed vector is valid. Pre-filtering has no index over the filtered subset, degenerating toward brute force. Post-filtering discards non-matches after the unfiltered search, which can silently under-return since the greedy search never routed toward the filter-valid region.

drills.q: Walk through the mechanism of post-filter under-return with a concrete number.
drills.a: A filter matching ~10% of the corpus with ef_search=40 retrieves on average only ~4 filter-valid candidates by chance, well short of a k=10 request, even though far more valid matches exist elsewhere in the graph that the search never routed toward.

drills.q: Define cardinality and selectivity. Why is a high-cardinality filter the expensive case for both strategies?
drills.a: Cardinality is the number of distinct values a field can take; selectivity is what fraction of the corpus one value matches. A high-cardinality field like tenant_id (millions of values) produces high selectivity per value -- worst case for pre-filter (small unindexed scan) and post-filter (severe under-return).

drills.q: Why must ACL filtering be enforced in the retrieval query itself rather than as a post-retrieval check?
drills.a: If unauthorized documents are retrieved and filtered out afterward in application code, they may already be logged, cached, briefly present in a response payload, or exposed via a timing/count side-channel before the discard runs. The ineligible data must never leave the boundary, not merely be removed before a user notices.

drills.q: Compare RBAC and ABAC for retrieval filtering, and explain why production systems move toward ABAC.
drills.a: RBAC attaches permissions to roles -- simple, coarse-grained. ABAC computes permissions from user/resource/context attributes, supporting finer-grained dynamic rules (e.g. department match AND clearance level). Systems move toward ABAC as access rules grow more contextual, but often layer both rather than replacing RBAC entirely.

drills.q: Why is oversampling before post-filtering only a mitigation and not a fix?
drills.a: It increases the chance enough filter-valid results appear in a larger candidate set, but doesn't change the underlying mechanism -- the search still isn't routing toward the filter-valid region deliberately, so a selective enough filter (or too-small oversample factor) can still under-return, at proportionally higher compute cost.

drills.q: A pgvector-backed filtered query that used to return in milliseconds now takes seconds. What's your diagnostic path?
drills.a: Check whether filter selectivity changed (new tenant, data growth) pushing the query from a cheap high-selectivity case into one requiring hnsw.iterative_scan or a partial index/partition. Confirm by measuring current selectivity directly. If selectivity is unchanged, check for index bloat from tombstoned HNSW deletions or concurrent write contention.

drills.q: Design the metadata schema and multi-tenancy strategy for a SaaS RAG product with tenants ranging from 100 to 5 million documents.
drills.a: Denormalize tenant_id, ACL, and filterable fields onto chunk records. Given the four-order-of-magnitude skew, tier by size: smallest tenants use brute-force/in-memory search; mid-size tenants share a filter-aware index (ACORN-style or iterative scan); largest tenants get dedicated physical index isolation. ACL is enforced as a query-time filter in all three tiers, never post-retrieval.

drills.q: A customer reports search results including another customer's tenant data after a routine ingest pipeline update. Walk through your incident response.
drills.a: Treat it as a security incident first: determine immediately whether the ACL/tenant filter is a query-time condition or a post-retrieval check -- if post-retrieval, that's very likely root cause. Check whether the ingest change altered tenant_id/ACL denormalization (sync bug, race condition during backfill). Audit logs/caches for whether leaked data was already exposed downstream, not just currently visible. Remediate by moving enforcement to query-time filtering and adding database-level row-level security as defense-in-depth.

drills.q: Why is schema evolution usually cheap when adding a new filterable field, but risky when changing an existing field's type or semantics?
drills.a: Adding a field is typically a metadata backfill only -- the vector is unaffected, no re-embedding required. Changing type/semantics (boolean to enum) requires auditing every dependent code path and index assumption, and partial rollout can produce silently inconsistent filtering -- needs a transitional sentinel state and validated 100% backfill before cutover.
